CLASS 36 · AGES 4–5 · 22 HABITAT LESSONS

Animals & Their Habitats.

HOW THIS CLASS WORKS

Twenty-two animals, twenty-two right homes.

Every animal in this class has its own step-by-step lesson: open the card together, find the animal and its home, say the habitat word, follow the teaching steps, ask the questions and finish with a game that puts your child inside that home — hopping the grassland, huddling like penguins, hanging like a bat. The order is gentle: homes near home first — the meadow and the pond — then the forests, the warm grasslands and the desert, the fresh and salt water, the freezing poles, and finally the dark cave.

One card a sitting is plenty; the whole class is a month of five-minute animal visits. By the end, the big question of early science — where does this animal live, and why THERE? — has twenty-two answered examples, from a rabbit in the tall grass to a whale in the deep blue.

A HOME FOR EVERY ANIMAL

Matching animals to their addresses.

Habitats are the first matching game in science: every animal carries its home in its body. The camel carries the desert in its feet and lashes, the polar bear wears the arctic as camouflage, the koala holds one tree in its tummy and its arms. Once your child can ask "could the whale live in the desert?" — and laugh at the answer — the whole set has done its work.

The cards love to be sorted. Lay them out and make home-piles: grass homes, tree homes, water homes, ice homes, the cave. Every sort is a different lesson, and no two children sort them quite the same way — all of them are right.

Twenty-two habitat cards, one picture each. Tap any picture and it opens its own lesson page — the original artwork with a drawing canvas on the left, and what the habitat is and why this animal fits it, taught step by step, on the right.

LEARNING PATH LESSON · ANIMALS & THEIR HABITATS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Rabbit — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches what a meadow actually is and why it suits the rabbit perfectly: dinner and a hiding place growing from the same soil, plus a burrow underneath for the night.

What is this?

A meadow is a field of tall grass and wildflowers that is allowed to grow long. No pavements, no lawn mower — just grass, stems, seeds and the small tunnels underneath.

What does it mean?

For a rabbit the tall growth does two jobs at the same time. It is food — rabbits nibble grass almost all day — and it is cover: a rabbit low in long grass is nearly invisible from above. Home that feeds you and hides you is a good home.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three meadow ideas: meadows are fields of tall grass, not empty gaps; the grass is the rabbit’s dinner and its hiding spot in one; and underneath it all the rabbit digs a burrow — a tunnel home where it sleeps and raises its babies.

Why this matters

The rabbit is the friendliest possible door into habitats, because children already know rabbits from stories. The discovery is that the rabbit in the book cannot actually live anywhere: it needs the meadow, specifically, and once a child sees that, every other animal-home pairing in this class starts making sense.

What it teaches

Habitat matching (animal to home), the idea that bodies suit their homes — big ears for hearing danger, strong back legs for hopping away — plus empathy through hiding play, and the first green word every ecologist needs: grassland.

Words to learn

meadowgrasstallhideburrownibblehop

Say this to your child

“"The rabbit lives in the meadow. The tall grass is its lunch and its hiding place at the same time — and underneath, the rabbit has dug a burrow where it sleeps. Nobody can see it from up high. That is why the meadow is the right home for a rabbit."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is a rabbit, and this is its home — a meadow."
  2. Say the two-job idea slowly: the tall grass is the rabbit’s food AND its hiding place. One plant, both jobs.
  3. Point at the picture: where could the burrow be? Under the green mound — the rabbit’s front door is a hole.
  4. Ask what the rabbit’s big ears and big back legs are for. Hearing danger early, and hopping away fast — the meadow rewards both.
  5. Finish with the crouch game (below) and one sentence to take away: "the rabbit lives in the meadow because the meadow feeds it and hides it."

Look closer at the picture

On this card a soft beige rabbit with pink-lined ears and a tiny smile sits calmly on a round green mound of grass. Behind it the sky is plain and pale, and the word "meadow" sits below — the rabbit is outdoors, low, and surrounded by exactly the green it eats.

Ask your child

"What does the rabbit eat in the meadow?" "Where does the grass hide the rabbit from?" "Where does the rabbit sleep at night — in a bed, or a hole?" "What are those big ears for?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "The grass is the rabbit’s food," "It hides in the tall grass so nobody sees it," or the burrow line: "It sleeps in a hole under the ground!"

Out in the real world

Find any unmown strip — a park edge, a roadside verge, a corner of the garden — and crouch down inside it. From rabbit height the grass is a roof overhead. That little flip of scale, forest of grass, is the meadow understood.

Try it together

Hide-the-rabbit: one player closes their eyes while the "rabbit" curls small behind grass-colored things or under a green blanket. The seeker gets one look from standing height only — then must find the rabbit by walking low. Hiding works better low. That is the whole meadow lesson, played.

Understanding check

Ask: "Where does a rabbit live? What are the two jobs of the tall grass? Where does it sleep?" Meadow, food-and-hiding, burrow — three answers and the lesson is home.

Parent tips

If your child worries the rabbit is lonely or scared out there, lean in: the burrow has a whole family in it. Meadow, food, family underground — rabbits live a small, warm life that children find very satisfying once it is described.

This lesson pairs with the Rabbit flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Animals & Their Habitats (Class 36).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · ANIMALS & THEIR HABITATS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Frog — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches what a pond is and why the frog is the animal that fits it best: a hunter that sits on the lily pads, swims when trouble comes, and raises its babies in the same quiet water.

What is this?

A pond is a small body of still water — smaller than a lake, big enough for lily pads, reeds, tadpoles and all the insects frogs eat. Ponds can be tiny: some fit in a garden.

What does it mean?

The frog is a two-home animal in one home: it breathes air and sits on the pads, but it swims like a champion and lays its eggs in the water. The pond feeds it flies, hides it underwater and raises its tadpoles. Every part of the frog’s day happens within one splash of the edge.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three pond ideas: ponds are small still waters with plants growing in and around them; frogs sit on lily pads by day and plop into the water when startled; and frog babies are tadpoles — little swimming dots that grow legs and turn into frogs right there in the pond.

Why this matters

The frog delivers the strangest, most memorable fact in the early habitat curriculum: it completely changes its body as it grows, from swimming tadpole to hopping frog — and it does it all inside one pond. Children who meet that transformation never forget that water is a living place.

What it teaches

Life-cycle sequencing (egg, tadpole, frog), the two-worlds idea of air and water, listening skills through croak-spotting, and gentle nerve — ponds are slimy, jumpy places and approaching them anyway is real confidence work.

Words to learn

pondlily padreedcroakploptadpoleswim

Say this to your child

“"The frog lives at the pond. It sits on the lily pad very, very still, and when anything comes close — plop! — into the water it goes. The pond is where it eats, swims and where it was a tadpole once, with no legs at all."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is a frog, and this is its home — a pond."
  2. Read the scene: the frog sits ON the water, not in it — that flat green pad is its chair. Ask what happens if a heron comes near. Plop! Straight into the water.
  3. Tell the baby story: frog eggs are laid in the pond, tiny tadpoles hatch and swim, and slowly they grow legs and hop out. The pond is the nursery.
  4. Practice the frog move: crouch small on an imaginary pad, sit very still, then leap and "plop" behind a cushion.
  5. Finish with the listening challenge — next pond visit, the game is to hear one croak.

Look closer at the picture

On this card a bright green frog with a wide smile and big dark eyes sits in the middle of a round lily pad. Two orange-tipped reeds stand at its sides and gentle green water spreads below. The word "pond" sits under the scene — everything the frog needs fits in this one still corner.

Ask your child

"Where does the frog sit?" "What does the frog do when someone comes close?" "What was the frog before it was a frog?" "Can we be that still?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "It sits on the lily pad," "Plop! It jumps in the water," or the life-cycle line: "It was a tadpole first — it swims and then it hops!"

Out in the real world

Any pond, park puddle-pool or even a fountain edge works for frog-spotting: approach on tiptoe, listen for croaks, scan the pads. Most city ponds have frogs; the tiptoe approach is what makes it work. If a real plop happens as you arrive — that WAS the frog.

Try it together

Plop-and-freeze: everyone is a frog on a cushion pad. One player is the heron, walking slow circles. When the heron looks your way — freeze on the pad. When it looks away — you may bob and ribbit. Caught mid-bob means you hop to a new pad. Stillness is the skill; giggling is allowed after.

Understanding check

Ask: "Where does a frog live? Where does it sit? What do we call its swimming babies?" Pond, lily pad, tadpoles — three answers and the lesson has landed.

Parent tips

Do not rush the tadpole story — it is the single best transformation children this age own, and retelling it in three scenes (egg, swimmer, hopper) builds narrative muscle. And if your child asks whether frogs sleep in the water: yes, half-in, half-out — a frog never really leaves the pond far behind.

Staying safe

Pond edges are slip-prone: at real water, one grown-up holds one small hand, always. Never lean over a pond alone, and wash hands after any pond-side play — frogs are lovely, pond water is not for fingers.

This lesson pairs with the Frog flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Animals & Their Habitats (Class 36).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · ANIMALS & THEIR HABITATS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Squirrel — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches what woodland is and how the squirrel earns its living there: climbing, collecting and caching — and how the squirrel’s forgetfulness quietly grows the next forest.

What is this?

Woodland is a landscape of many trees with open, airy ground between them — lighter and bushier than deep forest. Acorns, seeds and mushrooms grow there, and tree trunks stand like apartment towers.

What does it mean?

For the squirrel the woodland is a supermarket that closes in winter. All autumn it gathers nuts and hides them in hundreds of separate spots — and in winter it digs them up again. The trees feed the squirrel; the squirrel spreads the trees. Two neighbours helping each other without knowing it.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three woodland ideas: woodland is tree-country with food on the ground; squirrels prepare for winter by hiding nuts in many secret places; and some hidden nuts are never found again — those grow into new trees.

Why this matters

The squirrel teaches foresight — work now, eat later — which is a genuinely new idea for four-year-olds, delivered by a twitchy, charming animal. The accidental-forester twist adds a cause-and-effect gem: today’s lost acorn is next century’s oak.

What it teaches

Planning and future thinking ("winter is coming — gather now"), spatial memory through hiding games, tree-part vocabulary (trunk, branch, acorn), and the mutual-help idea that runs all through nature.

Words to learn

woodlandacorngatherhidewintertrunkstash

Say this to your child

“"The squirrel lives in the woodland. All autumn it gathers acorns and hides them in secret places for winter. It forgets some of them — and those grow into new trees! The squirrel is the forest’s little gardener without knowing it."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is a squirrel, and this is its home — the woodland."
  2. Point at the acorn in the paws: the squirrel is holding its winter plans. In autumn it hides hundreds of nuts — not one big pile, but hundreds of little secret stashes.
  3. Tell the twist: the squirrel forgets some of them. Those forgotten nuts sleep in the ground and wake up as baby trees. Squirrels plant forests by accident.
  4. Ask where the squirrel lives in the trees — up in a drey, a round leafy nest, high in the branches.
  5. Play the gather-and-remember game (below), then close with the cycle: tree makes nuts, squirrel hides nuts, forgotten nuts make new trees.

Look closer at the picture

On this card a red-brown squirrel with a cream chest and tufted ears holds one acorn in both front paws, sitting beside a thick brown trunk with a leafy branch overhead. The word "woodland" sits below — tree, squirrel and acorn, the whole partnership in one scene.

Ask your child

"What is the squirrel holding?" "Why does it hide nuts instead of eating them all now?" "What happens to the nuts it forgets?" "Where up in the tree does it sleep?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "It hides acorns for winter," "It forgot some — they grow into trees!" or the proud memory claim: "I can find all five of mine!"

Out in the real world

Under any big tree in autumn, hunt for acorns and half-eaten stashes — teeth marks on a dropped acorn are squirrel evidence. In parks, watch real squirrels dig, pause, and dig elsewhere: a cache being checked, or a fake burial to fool watchers.

Try it together

Gather-and-remember: hide five "acorns" around a room while your child watches, then send the little squirrel to gather them all into one stash. Next round, your child hides and you gather. Hardest round: hide them, play something else for ten minutes, then search — winter is long and squirrels’ memories are tested by time.

Understanding check

Ask: "Where does a squirrel live? What does it do all autumn? What grows from its forgotten nuts?" Woodland, hides nuts, new trees — three answers and the pantry is stocked.

Parent tips

Let your child be better than the squirrel — remembering all five is a real triumph worth a cheer. The forget-some part is not failure; it is the forest’s plan. Keep that framing warm: mistakes that grow trees are the best kind.

This lesson pairs with the Squirrel flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Animals & Their Habitats (Class 36).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · ANIMALS & THEIR HABITATS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Fox — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches how the fox uses the woodland differently from the squirrel: same trees, opposite timetable. The fox sleeps through the day and owns the quiet hours — with ears that hear everything and feet that make no sound at all.

What is this?

A fox lives where the woodland meets the open: hedgerows, thickets, bramble corners — good hiding near good hunting. Its den is a hole or a sheltered hollow where cubs are born and days are slept away.

What does it mean?

Two animals can share one woodland by working different shifts. The squirrel works all day; the fox starts at dusk. Big triangle ears catch the smallest squeak in the grass, and paws built for silence let the fox arrive before anything hears it. The woodland offers night and day — the fox took the night.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three fox ideas: foxes make dens in quiet corners at the woodland edge; they are most active at dusk and dawn, not midday; and their tools are giant ears, sharp eyes and feet so soft that nothing hears them coming.

Why this matters

The fox gently breaks a pattern: not every animal’s day looks like ours. Meeting an animal whose "morning" is our bedtime stretches a child’s imagination of time itself — and the fox’s famous cleverness becomes concrete when it is explained as ears plus patience plus quiet feet.

What it teaches

Time concepts (day shift and night shift), sound awareness through listening games, body-tool reasoning (ears, eyes, feet), and gentle courage — foxes are the animals children both love and find just a little bit spooky, and understanding dissolves the spooky.

Words to learn

foxdenduskquiettrotbushysharp ears

Say this to your child

“"The fox lives at the woodland edge, in a den among the bushes. It sleeps in the day, and when the sun goes down it trots out on soft, silent feet. Its big ears hear everything — that is how the fox feeds its family at night."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is a fox, and this is where it lives — the edge of the woodland."
  2. Compare shifts: the squirrel naps at night; the fox naps by day and goes trotting when the sky turns orange. Same forest, different clock.
  3. Point at the ears: those triangles catch the tiniest sounds — a mouse’s squeak from far away in the grass.
  4. Do the ears test right now: whisper from across the room and watch how fast your child’s fox ears find you.
  5. Finish with silent feet practice — fox-walk across the room without one creak. If someone hears you, back to the den and try again.

Look closer at the picture

On this card an orange fox with a white chest, black ear-tips and black boots sits calmly in short green grass, a pine tree and round bushes behind it, under a pale blue sky. The word "woodland" sits below — the fox is resting between its night shifts, right at the trees’ soft edge.

Ask your child

"When does the fox wake up — morning or evening?" "How do its feet help it hunt?" "What do those big ears hear?" "Where does a fox sleep through the day?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "The fox sleeps in the day," "Its feet are so quiet nobody hears it," or the ears line: "It hears a mouse far away with those big ears!"

Out in the real world

At dusk, open a window and listen for fox sounds — a short sharp bark carries far in the evening quiet. In towns too: foxes live along garden edges and railway lines. Early morning paw prints in soft ground tell last night’s trotting route.

Try it together

Fox-and-feathers: one player is the fox and must cross the room and lift a toy from a shelf without the "rabbits" (lying on the floor, eyes closed) hearing a single step. Any twitch of the rabbits’ ears sends the fox back to the den. Silence is the whole game — and the whole fox.

Understanding check

Ask: "When is the fox busy — day or night? How does it walk? What do its ears do?" Night, silent feet, hear everything — three answers and the den is warm.

Parent tips

If your child finds foxes a bit frightening, lead with competence, not creepiness: the fox is not sneaky for fun, it is a parent bringing food home to cubs in a den. A tired working parent with excellent ears is a very friendly monster to be.

This lesson pairs with the Fox flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Animals & Their Habitats (Class 36).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · ANIMALS & THEIR HABITATS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Owl — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the owl’s version of forest life: perched high above the floor, watching with the biggest eyes in the bird world and gliding down through the dark without a whisper of wing.

What is this?

A forest is deeper and darker than woodland — tall trunks close together, layered from floor to canopy. Owls claim the middle-height branches, and older trees offer hollows: ready-made dark rooms for sleeping the day away.

What does it mean?

The forest stacks life in floors: roots below, moss and mice on the ground, branches in the middle, leaves on top. The owl rents the middle floor and hunts the bottom one — from a branch with a clear view, its giant eyes gather light so well that night looks like late evening up there. When it hears a move below, it drops silently and the forest floor never hears it coming.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three owl ideas: owls perch on branches and rest in tree hollows by day; their huge eyes see in near-dark, and they turn their whole heads to look around; and their wing feathers are fringed so soft that flight makes no sound at all.

Why this matters

The owl reframes "night is scary" into "night has its own experts". Children meet the dark through an animal that is not just unafraid but spectacularly good at it — the forest at night becomes a workplace with the owl on shift, and bedtime stops being when the world ends.

What it teaches

Vertical thinking (habitat layers: floor, branch, canopy), light-and-dark science, head-turn body awareness, listening precision, and comfort with darkness built through the night-shift framing.

Words to learn

owlbranchhollowglidesilenttwilighthoot

Say this to your child

“"The owl lives high in the forest. By day it rests in a hollow tree; by night its great golden eyes watch the ground below. Its wings make no sound at all — the mouse on the forest floor never hears a thing until the owl is there."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is an owl, and this is its home — high in the forest trees."
  2. Point at the eyes: those two big golden circles catch even the tiny light of the moon and stars. To the owl, night is never fully dark.
  3. Try the owl neck: eyes fixed forward, turn only your head slowly left and right. That is how owls look around — their eyes cannot swivel, so the head does the travelling.
  4. Do the silent-wing test with a scarf or tea towel: flap it fast (whoosh!) then slow and wide. Owls fly slow and wide — soft, silent, unbeatable for sneaking.
  5. Finish with the listen-and-swoop game (below) and one line: "the owl sleeps by day in a hollow and rules the forest at night."

Look closer at the picture

On this card a brown owl with a cream, speckled chest and two enormous golden eyes grips a leafy branch with its talons, dark pine trees standing behind it. The word "forest" sits below — perched, patient and facing us, the owl is exactly where a forest puts its night watch.

Ask your child

"Why are the owl’s eyes so big?" "What sound do its wings make?" "Where does it sleep during the day?" "Can you turn your head like an owl?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Its eyes see in the dark," "Its wings are silent — whoosh, no sound!" or the head-turn boast: "I can look behind me like an owl!"

Out in the real world

At twilight, stand under tall trees and hoot-listen for one minute — many parks have owls that call right after sunset. By day, look for owl pellets and pale droppings on trunks below hollows: the quiet evidence of the night shift.

Try it together

Listen-and-swoop: the "mouse" rustles a paper under a blanket while the owl sits blindfolded (or eyes-closed) on a chair-branch. One rustle, then stillness — the owl points to where the sound came from, then swoops (arms wide, silent, no whooshing — owls never whoosh) to catch it. Score a point for silence on the swoop.

Understanding check

Ask: "Where does the owl perch? What do its big eyes do? How do its wings fly?" On a branch, see in the dark, silently — three answers and the forest sleeps safe.

Parent tips

Own the head-turn yourself first — children copy the owl neck for days once it is taught, and every repetition rehearses the lesson. If the dark still feels big, end with this: somewhere out there, an owl is flying right now and it thinks the dark is easy.

This lesson pairs with the Owl flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Animals & Their Habitats (Class 36).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · ANIMALS & THEIR HABITATS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Koala — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the most specialised home in the class: the koala lives in eucalyptus forest because eucalyptus leaves — poisonous to almost everyone else — are its one and only meal.

What is this?

A eucalyptus forest is a woodland of gum trees: smooth pale trunks, long silver-green leaves and a smell like cough sweets when the sun warms them. These trees grow across great stretches of Australia.

What does it mean?

Eucalyptus leaves are full of strong oils — most animals that eat them get a very bad tummy. The koala’s gut is built exactly for those oils, so a leaf that is poison to others is dinner to the koala. That one trick means nobody else wants its food, and its forest stays its own: one tree, one animal, one perfect match.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three koala ideas: eucalyptus trees have special leaves most animals cannot eat; the koala’s tummy CAN — that is its superpower; and because its food is low-energy, the koala saves strength by sleeping up to twenty hours a day, hugging its branch.

Why this matters

The koala is the class’s cleanest specialist: where the rabbit eats many things and the fox many more, the koala eats one — and the lesson that bodies can be shaped to fit one home, one food, one place is the deep idea behind every habitat on Earth.

What it teaches

Specialist-versus-generalist reasoning (first form!), cause and effect (oily leaves, koala tummy), grip-strength body awareness, and the calm lesson that slow and sleepy is a strategy, not laziness.

Words to learn

koalaeucalyptusgum treeleaveshuggripsleepy

Say this to your child

“"The koala lives in the eucalyptus forest. Its leaves would make most animals sick, but the koala’s tummy is built just for them. It eats, then it hugs a branch and sleeps — nearly the whole day. One tree is its whole world."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is a koala, and this is its home — the eucalyptus forest."
  2. Hold the superpower reveal for the big moment: these leaves would give most animals a terrible tummy — but the koala’s tummy is built for exactly them. Poison to others, lunch to the koala.
  3. Explain the sleepy part: those leaves are not very filling, so the koala saves energy by sleeping nearly all day, hugging its branch high in the tree.
  4. Point at the paws on the card: two thumbs for gripping — made for hugging trunks.
  5. Do the koala hug (below), then close with the match: gum tree, koala tummy — made for each other.

Look closer at the picture

On this card a fluffy grey koala with big round ears and a black nose hugs a slanted eucalyptus branch, leafy sprigs rising on both sides of the picture. The words "eucalyptus forest" sit below — one animal, one tree, holding on.

Ask your child

"What does the koala eat?" "Could a fox eat these leaves?" "Why does the koala sleep so much?" "How many thumbs does a koala have on each paw?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "It eats the leaves from the gum tree," "Other animals get sick but koalas don’t!" or the sleepy line: "It sleeps almost all day hugging the tree."

Out in the real world

Crush one eucalyptus leaf near a florist’s greens or a gum tree if you have one, and sniff — that strong medicine smell is the very oil that upsets other tummies. Koalas eat the smell. That connection lands harder than any explanation.

Try it together

Koala hug contest: everyone claims a "trunk" — a doorframe, a table leg, a grown-up — grips on with both hands and holds through a slow count of twenty without slipping. Winner gets the koala nap: ten seconds of seated dozing on the spot. Grip, then sleep. That is the daily koala routine, played.

Understanding check

Ask: "Which tree is the koala’s home? What do other animals think of its leaves? What does the koala do all day?" Eucalyptus, sick, sleep-and-hug — three answers and the lesson sticks like a koala on a branch.

Parent tips

Do not rush past "poison to others, dinner to the koala" — it is a jaw-dropper and deserves a pause. If your child then asks whether koalas are lazy, hold the line kindly: sleeping IS the koala’s smart plan; it keeps the small food budget balanced.

This lesson pairs with the Koala flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Animals & Their Habitats (Class 36).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · ANIMALS & THEIR HABITATS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Panda — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches what a bamboo forest is and how the panda lives in it: cool mountain air, green stalks everywhere, and a bear that turned eating leaves into a full-time job.

What is this?

A bamboo forest is a stand of bamboo — giant grasses as tall as trees, growing in thick green clusters high on cool, often misty mountains. Bamboo grows so fast it can almost be watched growing.

What does it mean?

Bamboo is mostly water and fibre — filling, but not very rich. So the panda’s strategy is volume: sit among the stalks and eat, for most waking hours, day after day. The forest never runs out, the panda never stops, and the misty mountains keep it all cool and green.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three bamboo-forest ideas: bamboo is giant grass, not a tree; pandas eat bamboo for breakfast, lunch and dinner — and most snacks between; and pandas have a special wrist bone that works like a thumb for gripping the stalks.

Why this matters

The panda pairs beautifully with the koala: two specialists, two one-food lives, one cool forest and one warm one. Children meet the idea that a habitat is not just an address but a menu — and that a big strong bear can be a gentle, patient, all-day nibbler.

What it teaches

Diet thinking (what fills you up and why), contrast reasoning (bear expectation versus panda reality), grip mechanics, and pacing — the slow-and-steady eating marathon is a patience model children can feel at snack time.

Words to learn

pandabamboostalkmistymountainsmunchgrip

Say this to your child

“"The panda lives in the bamboo forest, high on the cool mountains. It is a big strong bear that eats bamboo all day — crunch, crunch, crunch. Its wrist has a special thumb just for holding the stalks."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is a panda, and this is its home — the bamboo forest."
  2. Reveal the surprise: this is a BEAR — big and strong — but it does not hunt. It munches grass. Giant grass: bamboo, tall as trees.
  3. Explain the all-day part: bamboo does not pack much power, so the panda eats and eats — most of its day is breakfast, lunch and dinner rolled together.
  4. Point at the front paws: a panda’s wrist bone works like a sixth finger, made for gripping bamboo stalks.
  5. Play the panda snack (below) and close with the picture: cool mist, green towers, one contented bear munching.

Look closer at the picture

On this card a round black-and-white panda walks on all fours across a green patch, tall bamboo stalks rising on every side under a soft pale sky. The words "bamboo forest" sit below — the panda is strolling through its own enormous salad bar.

Ask your child

"What is the panda eating?" "Is bamboo a tree or giant grass?" "How much of the panda’s day is eating?" "What does its special wrist bone do?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "It eats bamboo all day long," "Bamboo is giant grass — taller than Dad!" or the wrist line: "It has a thumb on its wrist for holding the bamboo!"

Out in the real world

At the fruit bowl, compare a juicy grape (rich, small) with a stick of celery (filling, plain) — celery is your household bamboo. One bite fills a little; a panda needs the whole forest. Rich foods make quick meals; plain foods make long ones.

Try it together

Panda picnic: serve a "bamboo" snack — breadsticks, celery sticks or green beans — and eat it panda-style: sitting cross-legged, stalk held in both front paws, chomped sideways from the end. Timer optional, but one stalk must be finished properly before any jumping. All-day eaters eat slowly.

Understanding check

Ask: "Where does the panda live? What does it eat? What helps it grip the stalks?" Bamboo forest, bamboo, the wrist-thumb — three answers and the picnic is packed.

Parent tips

Hold the contrast with other bears gently — yes, some bears hunt, but the panda found a forest full of food nobody else wanted and made it a kingdom. If your child asks why pandas do not eat something richer: the forest only serves bamboo, and the panda likes what its home serves.

This lesson pairs with the Panda flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Animals & Their Habitats (Class 36).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · ANIMALS & THEIR HABITATS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Monkey — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the rainforest as a layered world and the monkey as its treetop specialist: up in the canopy the light is good, the fruit is sweet and the floor belongs to somebody else entirely.

What is this?

A rainforest is a tall, thick, wet forest — the hottest, greenest habitat on Earth. Its trees stand so close and grow so high that they lock branches into a roof called the canopy, where most rainforest animals spend their whole lives.

What does it mean?

Down on the forest floor it is dim, damp and hard to move; up in the canopy it is bright, fruity and full of highways — branches, vines and lianas laid out like roads. The monkey’s whole design answers the canopy: gripping hands and feet, a balancing tail, eyes that judge every jump. The troop travels the treetops together, chattering news of the ripest fruit.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three rainforest ideas: rainforests are tall, wet, crowded forests full of life; the canopy — the treetop roof — is where monkeys live, not the ground; and monkeys move in troops, families that travel, eat and watch out for each other together.

Why this matters

The rainforest gives children the single most useful habitat idea in the class: a home can have floors, and different animals live on different floors of the same forest. Once the canopy-versus-floor split is clear, the owl, the panda and every forest card after it gains a map.

What it teaches

Layer thinking (floor, middle, canopy), grip-and-balance body awareness, group-living concepts (troop, family, watch-out-for-each-other), and jumping judgement — the same skill a monkey’s next branch demands.

Words to learn

rainforestcanopytreetopvinetroopgripswing

Say this to your child

“"The monkey lives in the rainforest — but not on the ground. Up in the treetops the branches are its roads and the fruit is its shop. It travels with its family, hand over hand, and its tail helps it hold on."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is a monkey, and this is its home — the rainforest, up in the treetops."
  2. Build the layers with your hands: one hand low — dark, damp forest floor; other hand high — the canopy, where the sun gets through. The monkey lives up top.
  3. Point at the tail: curled like a hook. It balances and grips, a fifth hand for the high roads.
  4. Explain the troop: monkeys never travel alone — the family moves together, calls together and shares the fruit it finds.
  5. Play the canopy crossing (below) and close with the map: floor for the shy ones, canopy for the monkey.

Look closer at the picture

On this card a cheerful brown monkey with a lighter face and belly sits among deep green leaves, its long tail curling up behind it in a question-mark hook. The word "rainforest" sits below — deep in the green, well above the forest floor.

Ask your child

"Where does the rainforest monkey live — on the floor or in the trees?" "What is its tail for?" "Who does it travel with?" "What is the canopy?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "It lives up in the trees," "Its tail holds on like a hook," or the troop line: "Monkeys go everywhere together, with their family!"

Out in the real world

Playground frames are canopy simulators — climbing them IS rainforest practice, and saying so mid-climb ("you are in the canopy right now!") turns the bars into a habitat. Vine and liana talk works at any rope or swing.

Try it together

Canopy crossing: tape a start and finish line and rule the floor off-limits — canopy travellers cross only by climbing, reaching and balancing along sofas, cushions and mats (grown-up spotting, of course). Touch the floor and it is a gentle "down to the forest floor — climb back up!" Reaching the far tree earns the fruit.

Understanding check

Ask: "Where does the monkey live in the rainforest? What is the treetop roof called? Who does it travel with?" In the trees, the canopy, its troop — three answers and the lesson swings home.

Parent tips

Name the troop habit out loud whenever the family walks anywhere together — "we are moving like a troop, nobody gets left behind." The rainforest lesson sticks to family life. And if a child asks what is DOWN there on the floor: the shy ones — anteaters, jaguars, beetles. Different floors, different families.

This lesson pairs with the Monkey flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Animals & Their Habitats (Class 36).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · ANIMALS & THEIR HABITATS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Zebra — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches what a grassland is and how the zebra survives one: no hiding places out in the open, so the zebra wears its hiding place — a moving crowd of stripes that melts every hunter’s aim.

What is this?

A grassland is a huge stretch of grass with few trees and a sky that goes on forever — open, breezy country where grass grows taller than a toddler and herds can see trouble coming from far away.

What does it mean?

Out on the grassland there is nowhere to hide — so the zebras hide in each other. When a herd stands and moves together, the stripes run together into one flickering pattern, and a hunter’s eyes stop being able to say where one zebra ends and the next begins. The stripes also fit the light of tall grass: black, white and shadow-play.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three zebra ideas: grasslands are wide open grass countries with almost no trees; zebras live in herds and their stripes blur together when they move as one; and no two zebras share the same stripe pattern — each one is wearing its own name.

Why this matters

The zebra turns a weakness (nothing to hide behind) into the set’s most beautiful counter-trick, teaching children that safety can come from family togetherness as well as cover. It also plants the first "everyone is identifiable" idea: stripes like fingerprints.

What it teaches

Pattern and visual perception (what dazzles the eye), group behaviour (herd as shield), comparing open versus covered homes, and identity thinking — every zebra distinct, every pattern unique.

Words to learn

zebragrasslandherdstripesdazzletall grasshorizon

Say this to your child

“"The zebra lives on the grassland, where the grass grows tall and the sky goes on forever. There is nowhere to hide out here — so the zebras hide in each other! When they stand together, their stripes blur into one dazzle and nobody can tell where one zebra ends."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is a zebra, and this is its home — the grassland."
  2. Describe the openness: look how far the grass goes and how big the sky is. Out here there are no walls to hide behind — the zebra needs another trick.
  3. Do the dazzle demo (below): when many zebras stand together, their stripes run together like one wavy picture, and a hunter cannot tell where one zebra stops.
  4. Tell the name-secret: no two zebras wear the same stripes — a zebra knows its mummy in the herd by her pattern alone.
  5. Finish with herd stance: everyone huddles shoulder to shoulder, stripes together, faces out. That is the grassland trick: one pattern, many zebras.

Look closer at the picture

On this card a black-and-white striped zebra with a dark muzzle stands among tall green blades of grass that rise higher than its knees, under a soft pale sky. The word "grassland" sits below — one zebra, in grass, wearing a pattern as bold as its home is open.

Ask your child

"What does the grassland look like — full of trees or full of grass?" "Why do zebras stand together in a herd?" "How does a zebra know its mummy?" "What are the stripes doing when the herd runs?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "It lives in the tall grass with the big sky," "The stripes dazzle the hunters!" or the identity line: "Every zebra has different stripes — like names!"

Out in the real world

Zebra-striped things are everywhere once you look: crossings, rugs, jerseys. At every one, ask the dazzle question — "could you count the zebras in that pattern?" — and watch the idea travel from card to street. A real-optical moment: hold a striped bag against other patterns and see which eye wins.

Try it together

Stripe wave: three or more players (or one child plus soft toys) each hold a striped thing — sock, ribbon, scarf — and shuffle side to side in a line. The counter, ten steps away, must say exactly how many stripes-owners there are. Moving stripes, miscounted. That is the herd, played.

Understanding check

Ask: "Where does the zebra live? What is its trick for staying safe? Do two zebras share stripes?" Grassland, herd dazzle, never — three answers and the lesson stands out plain as stripes.

Parent tips

If your child asks why lions do not just watch one zebra, give the honest version: sometimes they manage — but the dazzle makes every bite of watching harder, and out on the grassland, every extra second of confusion is a zebra saved. Nature’s tricks raise the odds; they do not promise miracles.

This lesson pairs with the Zebra flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Animals & Their Habitats (Class 36).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · ANIMALS & THEIR HABITATS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Kangaroo — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the grassland from the kangaroo’s side: open, treeless miles where walking is too slow — so the kangaroo hops, carries its baby in a pouch and owns the bounce.

What is this?

The Australian grassland is wide open tussock country — clumps of coarse grass, scattered shrubs, endless sky. No forests to duck into, no corners to hide behind: a landscape of distance.

What does it mean?

In a home made of distance, slow feet go hungry. The kangaroo’s giant hind legs and springy tail make hopping cheaper the faster it goes — a living pogo that crosses the plains in great bounds. And the joey travels inside mum’s pouch: a moving bedroom on a bouncing mum, the safest seat on the grassland.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three kangaroo ideas: kangaroo country is open grass with far horizons; kangaroos hop — big feet and a balancing tail — and cannot walk backwards at all; and a joey baby rides in its mother’s pouch, drinking milk and peeking out.

Why this matters

The kangaroo answers a question every habitat asks — how do you move through THIS home? — with the funniest, bounciest answer in the set. It also sneaks in real physics: hopping is energy-saving at speed, backwards is impossible, and tails are balances, not extras.

What it teaches

Movement science (hop versus walk), energy ideas, body-part function (tail as prop and balance), and care concepts — the pouch as a first nursery, mother as transport, baby as passenger.

Words to learn

kangaroohoppouchjoeytailboundtussock

Say this to your child

“"The kangaroo lives on the open grassland. Its big feet are springs and its tail is a balance — it hops everywhere, faster and faster, and never walks backwards. Baby kangaroos ride along in the pouch, peeking out at the world."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is a kangaroo, and this is its home — the open grassland."
  2. Point at the legs: those feet are as long as the kangaroo’s arms — springs, built for bouncing across the miles.
  3. Reveal the two best facts in order: a kangaroo cannot walk backwards — try it yourself, the hop only goes forward — and the tail is a third leg for standing and steering.
  4. Tell the pouch story: a joey rides in mum’s pouch, popping its head out to watch the grass go by. A bedroom that hops.
  5. Hold the hop races (below) and close with the shape of the home: open country, long views, one bouncy specialist.

Look closer at the picture

On this card a tan kangaroo with tall ears, a cream belly and big long feet stands upright between clumps of spiky grass, tail resting behind it on the ground. The word "grassland" sits below — one kangaroo, standing tall in a home with nothing but grass and sky.

Ask your child

"How does a kangaroo move — walking or hopping?" "What are the big feet and the tail for?" "Can it walk backwards?" "Where does a joey ride?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "It hops with its big springy feet," "Kangaroos can’t go backwards!" or the pouch line: "The baby rides in mum’s pouch and peeks out!"

Out in the real world

Two hops of kangaroo physics hide in daily life: a ball bounces higher the harder it is thrown (bigger hops cost less per metre), and stairs without a banister feel like open grassland — long views, no handrails, balance doing the work. Name both when you meet them.

Try it together

Hop-course: tape a start line and lay three "tussock" cushions across the room. Rules of the plains: hopping only, feet together, hands up as little paws — touch a cushion and it is a forward bound over it, never a step. Backwards is out of bounds — kangaroos cannot, and neither can the racers. Fastest joey to the far grass wins a peek-from-the-pouch rest.

Understanding check

Ask: "Where does a kangaroo live? How does it move and why? Where does the joey ride?" Grassland, hops on springy feet, in the pouch — three answers and the race is won.

Parent tips

The cannot-hop-backwards fact is the retell-forever fact — children verify it on their own bodies all week, and every failed backwards attempt re-teaches the lesson. If hopping indoors is too bouncy, ten slow-motion bounds with silent landings is the polite-kangaroo version.

This lesson pairs with the Kangaroo flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Animals & Their Habitats (Class 36).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · ANIMALS & THEIR HABITATS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Elephant — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches what a savanna is and introduces the set’s biggest idea: some animals do not just live in their habitat — they look after it. The elephant digs, clears and paves the savanna for everyone.

What is this?

A savanna is hot open country — tall dry golden grass, scattered flat-topped acacia trees, a wet season and a dry one. It looks empty from far away and is full of life up close.

What does it mean?

Through the dry months, water hides underground — and the elephant hears it. Digging with tusks and feet, it opens water holes that zebra, birds and lions drink from too. Its heavy footsteps clear walking paths through the grass that other animals use as roads, and its dung plants seeds along the way. Take away the elephant and the savanna loses its gardener.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three savanna ideas: the savanna is golden grass with scattered trees, hot and open; elephants dig water holes that everyone drinks from in the dry season; and elephants live in family herds led by the oldest female — the matriarch, who remembers where the water is.

Why this matters

The elephant carries the class’s deepest idea — habitat shapers — in the friendliest wrapper. Children who accept "the elephant helps everyone" have met ecology’s keystone concept years early, through an animal they already adore.

What it teaches

Ecosystem thinking (one animal’s work serving many), memory and leadership respect (the matriarch), trunk coordination, and scale play — the savanna’s distances and the elephant’s size both beg to be paced out.

Words to learn

elephantsavannaherdwater holetrunkmatriarchacacia

Say this to your child

“"The elephant lives on the savanna. When the rain stays away, it digs water holes with its tusks — and the zebras, the birds and everyone else come to drink from the elephant’s well. The oldest grandmother leads the family there. She remembers the way."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is an elephant, and this is its home — the savanna."
  2. Read the scene: golden grass, one shady acacia, big grey resident in the middle. Hot country with a wet season and a dry one.
  3. Tell the digging story: in the dry months water hides underground. The elephant hears it, digs with its tusks — and opens a water hole the whole neighbourhood drinks from.
  4. Meet the herd: elephants walk in families, and the boss is the oldest grandmother — she remembers, year after year, exactly where the water waits.
  5. Play the trunk games (below) and close with the title: the savanna’s gardener, on duty.

Look closer at the picture

On this card a large grey elephant with pale tusks, wide ears and a curled trunk stands in golden grass beneath a flat-topped acacia tree, a dark green bush at its feet. The word "savanna" sits below — the biggest gardener, standing in the garden it keeps.

Ask your child

"What does the elephant dig with?" "Who drinks from the water holes it makes?" "Who leads the elephant family?" "What colour is the savanna grass?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "It digs wells with its tusks," "Everyone drinks the elephant’s water!" or the leader line: "The oldest grandma knows where the water is."

Out in the real world

Water-hole thinking works at any park tap or bird bath: "who else drinks here?" The savanna idea — one provider, many guests — maps straight onto the family kitchen too, and the matriarch’s job maps onto whoever in the family remembers where everything is kept.

Try it together

Trunk drills: move a sock across the room using only one arm as an elephant trunk — sweeping, curling and lifting, no hands allowed. Then the water-hole dig: bury a blue cloth in the sandpit and dig one-armed until the "water" shows, trumpet loudly, and lead the toy animals over in a line, oldest toy first. Gardener’s duties, played in full.

Understanding check

Ask: "Where does the elephant live? What does it dig, and who drinks it? Who leads the herd?" Savanna, water holes for everyone, the oldest grandmother — three answers and the well is open.

Parent tips

Do not skip the grandmother — leadership-by-memory is the fact children quote back most, and it dignifies every older person they know. If your child asks whether the elephant minds sharing its water: that is the whole point of the lesson — on the savanna, the digger digs for everybody.

This lesson pairs with the Elephant flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Animals & Their Habitats (Class 36).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · ANIMALS & THEIR HABITATS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Lion — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson corrects the biggest lion misconception before it settles: the king of the savanna is a champion rester. Hot hours belong to the shade, the pride naps together — and the prowling comes later, when the air cools.

What is this?

The savanna heats up hard in the middle of the day. Shade under an acacia, a warm patch of sand and a pile of family is what a lion’s daytime looks like: rest, doze, groom, repeat — with tufts of tall grass and green bush nearby.

What does it mean?

Hunting is expensive and midday heat is brutal — so the lion’s plan is timing. Sleep through the hot hours on a full stomach’s worth of patience; hunt at dusk and dawn when the air cools and the prey’s eyes struggle. The tawny coat matches the dry grass exactly, and the pride — the lion family — shares the shade, the cubs and the hunt.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three lion ideas: lions rest up to twenty hours a day, usually together in the shade; a lion family is called a pride and the lionesses do most of the hunting; and a lion’s tawny coat disappears against dry grass — camouflage it wears like a uniform.

Why this matters

The lion flips the loudest story children know (fierce, always chasing) into a truer one (patient, rested, tactical). That correction is a thinking lesson in itself: the real king of the savanna wins by resting well and timing well — not by roaring all day.

What it teaches

Energy and rest concepts (why hunters save their strength), time-of-day thinking (cool hours versus hot hours), family-structure vocabulary (pride, lioness, cub), and color-matching reasoning — coat against grass, disguise against background.

Words to learn

lionpridemaneshadeprowltawnyroar

Say this to your child

“"The lion lives on the savanna and rests in the shade nearly all day — the pride naps together, cubs and all. When the air turns cool, the lionesses rise, stretch and prowl through the tall grass, quiet as shadows, their coats the very colour of home."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is a lion, and this is its home — the savanna."
  2. Flip the story gently: the lion looks fierce — and it is — but its favourite thing is a very long nap in the shade. Up to twenty hours a day.
  3. Ask why: hunting is hard work, midday is hot, and big runners overheat. So the pride rests together and hunts in the cool of morning and evening.
  4. Point at the coat: golden-tawny, exactly the colour of dry grass. Standing still, a lion half vanishes — the grass hides it.
  5. Meet the pride: lionesses hunt together; cubs tumble in the shade; the big dark mane says "grown-up". Finish by playing prowl-then-nap (below).

Look closer at the picture

On this card a golden lion with a full dark-brown mane and a calm, friendly face sits upright on warm sand, green shrubs and pale sky behind it, tail curled at its side. The word "savanna" sits below — the king at rest, between patrols.

Ask your child

"What is the lion doing most of the day?" "Why does it rest in the shade?" "What is a lion family called?" "Which lions do most of the hunting?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "It naps in the shade — twenty hours!" "The daddy lion has the big dark mane," or the prowl line: "The lionesses hunt together when it gets cool."

Out in the real world

Shade mathematics is everywhere: on a hot day, measure the cool with your child — under the tree versus on the path, one hand each. The lion’s midday plan is a park-bench plan. And at dusk, point out when the birds and bats swap shifts: the cool hours belong to the prowlers.

Try it together

Prowl-then-nap: everyone lies in a shade pile for a slow count of twenty — proper pride napping, shoulders touching. Then the lionesses rise, stretch long, and prowl one silent circle of the room, feet soft, bodies low. Only after the prowl comes the roar — one big family roar, then straight back to the nap. Energy saved, timing learned.

Understanding check

Ask: "Where does the lion spend the hot hours? What is its family called? What colour is its coat, and what does it match?" In the shade, a pride, tawny like the grass — three answers and the pride sleeps on.

Parent tips

Keep the mane clear without fuss: it is a grown-up boy-lion feature, the way a beard is. And if your child is disappointed the lion naps so much, lean in — that is the twist the whole lesson hangs on: the mightiest cat on the savanna wins by being still. Rest is not the opposite of fierce; it is what makes it possible.

This lesson pairs with the Lion flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Animals & Their Habitats (Class 36).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · ANIMALS & THEIR HABITATS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Camel — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the desert as a real home — hot, dry, wide and full of sand — and walks through the camel’s equipment piece by piece, starting with the biggest mix-up of all: what the hump actually holds.

What is this?

A desert is a land of very little rain — rolling dunes, bare rock, blazing days and chilly nights. Few plants grow, water hides in rare wells and oases, and the sand itself shifts with the wind.

What does it mean?

Every desert problem has a camel part as its answer. Scorching sun: long eyelashes and closable nostrils keep the sand out. Burning ground: wide padded feet that spread on soft sand like snowshoes. Long empty miles between wells: a hump that stores fat — not water! — to burn as travel fuel. The camel is not just in the desert; the desert is written all over it.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three desert ideas: deserts are the driest lands on Earth, all sand, rock and rare water; the camel’s hump stores fat for the long journey — not water; and its feet, lashes and nostrils are each a piece of desert equipment.

Why this matters

The camel delivers body-part reasoning at its clearest: hold up a problem (sun, sand, distance), name the part that solves it. Children learn to read an animal like a toolbox — a habit of thinking that transfers to every animal they will ever meet.

What it teaches

Problem-and-solution matching, sun-safety parallels (lashes like sunglasses, shade-seeking), balance skills through dune-walking games, and myth-busting confidence — your child now knows something most grown-ups get wrong.

Words to learn

cameldeserthumpduneoasislashespadded feet

Say this to your child

“"The camel lives in the desert, where the sun is hot and the sand goes on and on. Its hump is full of fat, not water — food for the long walk. Its lashes keep the sand out, its wide feet stay on top of the dunes, and on it goes, mile after mile."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is a camel, and this is its home — the desert."
  2. Fix the mix-up first, proudly: everyone says the hump holds water. It does not — it holds FAT, packed fuel for the long walk between wells.
  3. Run the equipment check: long lashes and shut-tight nostrils against the sand; wide spongy feet that grip soft dunes; knees built to kneel on hot ground.
  4. Explain the distance: in the desert, wells and oases sit far apart — the camel is the animal that crosses the gap and arrives ready for more.
  5. Play the dune walk (below) and close with the summary: sun, sand, distance — a part for every problem.

Look closer at the picture

On this card a sandy-tan camel with one neat hump, a short mane and a gentle face stands on firm sand, rolling dunes rising behind it under a pale clear sky. The word "desert" sits below — one traveller, at home between the dunes.

Ask your child

"What does the hump really store?" "Why does the desert not bother the camel’s eyes?" "Why are its feet so wide?" "What do we call a green, watery spot in the desert?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "The hump is fat, not water — for the long walk!" "Its lashes stop the sand," or the feet line: "Wide feet so it doesn’t sink in the sand!"

Out in the real world

Sun-gear comparison works anywhere bright: sunglasses as lashes, hat as shade-seek, water bottle as oasis plan. On sand at a beach or sandpit, test the feet rule yourself — flat hands or shoes sink less than heels. The camel’s engineering is kid-testable.

Try it together

Dune walk: lay a line of cushions or a strip of tape as a "dune ridge". Camel rules: heel-to-toe, arms out, eyes up — wobble off and it is back to the start oasis. Round two carries cargo (a beanbag on the head — the hump). Steady, wide, unhurried: the camel gait is the winning gait.

Understanding check

Ask: "What does the hump store? Name two camel parts that beat the desert. Where does a camel walk between?" Fat, lashes-and-wide-feet, well to well — three answers and the caravan moves on.

Parent tips

Let your child correct YOU on the hump at least once — act the mistake ("the hump is full of water, right?") and enjoy the triumphant "NO — FAT!". Being the family expert on one fact is a memory glue no drill can match.

Staying safe

Desert talk is sun-safety talk: hats, water and shade are the human version of lashes and humps. On real hot days, drink before thirsty and never play unattended near water — even the oasis has rules.

This lesson pairs with the Camel flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Animals & Their Habitats (Class 36).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · ANIMALS & THEIR HABITATS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Beaver — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson introduces the one animal in the class that constructs its own habitat: the beaver fells sticks, dams the stream, and pools the river into a pond deep enough to hide a front door under water.

What is this?

A river is moving fresh water — running from hills to sea, edged with reeds, willows and stones. It flows, it ripples and it changes its banks with every season.

What does it mean?

Moving water is a poor bedroom — so the beaver changes the speed. It drags branches and stones into the stream, packs the gaps with mud, and the backed-up water spreads into a still pond. In the middle it builds its lodge: a dome of sticks with the entrance UNDER the water, safe from hungry visitors. One busy builder, and the running river becomes a quiet, deep, private home.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three beaver ideas: rivers are running fresh water with grassy banks; beavers build dams from sticks and mud that turn the flow into a pond; and they live in a lodge with an underwater front door, reached by diving.

Why this matters

The beaver is engineering made visible at bath-toy scale: block the flow, still the water, build the house. It is also the set’s bridge between habitats — the beaver’s pond becomes frog-and-fish housing, planting the idea that one builder’s work opens homes for many.

What it teaches

Construction play and sequencing (gather, stack, pack), cause-and-effect with real water, tool reasoning (teeth as axes, tails as rudders), and generosity concepts — building that benefits the whole neighbourhood.

Words to learn

beaverriverdamlodgepondpaddle tailsticks

Say this to your child

“"The beaver lives by the river — but first it fixes the river. It piles up sticks and mud until the water stops and makes a pond, then builds a round stick house with its door hidden under the water. Dive in, pop up inside: home. And the new pond welcomes everyone."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is a beaver, and this is its home — the riverbank."
  2. State the problem like a builder: rivers RUN — too fast for a quiet house. So the beaver does something no other animal here does: it rebuilds the river.
  3. Walk the build: drag sticks and stones into the water, pack the gaps with mud — the water backs up and spreads into a still pond. That wall is called a dam.
  4. Tour the lodge: a dome of sticks in the pond, and the front door is UNDER the water — you get home by diving.
  5. Build a mini dam (below) and close with the generosity: the new pond becomes a home for frogs, fish and birds too.

Look closer at the picture

On this card a chestnut-brown beaver with a cream muzzle, two big front teeth and a flat paddle tail sits on a grassy bank beside blue water, reeds and bushes at the edges. The word "river" sits below — the builder on its own riverfront, sticks nearby.

Ask your child

"Why does a beaver build a dam?" "What is the dam made of?" "Where is the lodge’s door?" "Who else comes to live in the beaver’s pond?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "It blocks the river with sticks and mud," "Its door is under the water — it dives home!" or the neighbour line: "The pond is for the frogs and fish too!"

Out in the real world

Any flowing water is a beaver lecture: watch the current push a leaf and ask "could you build a house in water this fast? What would you do first?" Concrete tip: look for gnawed sticks and stumps with tooth-scarves — beaver country signs, in real parks.

Try it together

Bath or basin dam: tilt a slow trickle from the tap or a jug, then let your child stop it with a dam of twigs, duplo and foil, watching the water pool behind. Then the flood test — remove one stick and watch the leak teach engineering faster than any explanation. Dry-run version: build the dam with blocks across a hallway "river" of blue cloth.

Understanding check

Ask: "What does a beaver build first? What is the wall called? Where is the front door of the lodge?" A dam, sticks-and-mud, under the water — three answers and the pond is filling.

Parent tips

Say "engineer" out loud and often — a four-year-old who calls the beaver an animal engineer owns a word most meet at school age. And when the dam leaks, celebrate: leaks are how real dams teach. The beaver patches with mud; your child patches with one more block.

Staying safe

Real rivers and ponds earn the standing rule: grown-up hand within arm’s reach at any natural water, no leaning over banks, and hands washed after water play. The beaver dives safely; small people stay on the bank.

This lesson pairs with the Beaver flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Animals & Their Habitats (Class 36).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · ANIMALS & THEIR HABITATS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Turtle — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the coast as the meeting of two homes — land’s sand and sea’s waves — through the turtle, an animal that keeps one flipper in each: swimming all day, basking ashore, and hatching its babies right on the beach.

What is this?

The coast is where the sea meets the land: sandy beaches, wet sand at the wave-line, dunes behind, shallows ahead. It belongs to neither world and both at once.

What does it mean?

The turtle uses both halves of the coast. The sea feeds it — seagrass and jellyfish in the waves. The beach serves it — warm sand for basking, and, one night in a mother turtle’s life, the nursery: eggs buried in a sand nest above the tide-line, where the sun keeps them warm until the tiniest turtles dig out and dash for the waves.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three coast ideas: the coast is where beach meets sea — two habitats touching; sea turtles swim in the surf but rest on the sand; and baby turtles hatch from eggs buried in the dunes and walk to the water on their very first night.

Why this matters

The turtle holds the set’s first two-address life, and the baby-dash story is nature’s greatest cliffhanger — a journey every child can retell with their whole body. Coasts are also where most families actually meet the sea, so this card converts holidays into habitat lessons.

What it teaches

Two-category thinking (land home and water home in one life), sequencing the hatchling story, wave-and-sand sensory vocabulary, and empathy with fragility — the tiniest turtle against the gulls makes care feel urgent.

Words to learn

turtlecoastbeachwavesandnesthatchling

Say this to your child

“"The sea turtle lives at the coast, where the sand meets the sea. It swims among the waves all day and rests on the warm sand. And do you know where baby turtles are born? In a nest in the sand — then they dash to the sea, the very night they hatch!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is a sea turtle, and this is its home — the coast."
  2. Split the scene: one side sand, one side sea. Ask which half the turtle uses — and reveal the answer: both. Swim in the sea, rest on the sand.
  3. Tell the nursery story: a mother turtle hauls up at night, digs a nest above the waves with her back flippers, and buries her eggs in the warm sand.
  4. Tell the dash: weeks later the eggs hatch, and the tiniest turtles ever dig out and walk, wobble and sprint to the waves — their first journey, the night they are born.
  5. Play the hatchling dash (below) and close with the address: sea for lunch, beach for bed.

Look closer at the picture

On this card a green sea turtle with a patterned shell, scaly flippers and a smiling face rests on pale wet sand at the exact line where a gentle blue wave curls up the beach. The word "coast" sits below — half sand, half sea, both home.

Ask your child

"What are the two parts of the coast?" "What does the turtle do in the sea? On the sand?" "Where are turtle eggs laid?" "What do the babies do the night they hatch?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "It swims in the sea and sleeps on the beach," "The eggs are in a sand nest," or the dash line: "The babies run to the water as fast as they can, the first night!"

Out in the real world

Beach holidays become habitat audits with one question: which half is this — turtle sand or turtle sea? Wave-line footprints, tide marks and dune grass all feed the lesson, and any lifeguard-flag chat doubles as the safety briefing below.

Try it together

Hatchling dash: mark a "nest" line at one end of the room and a "sea" of blue cloth at the other. Hatchlings crouch low in the nest, count to three, then make the run — wobbly flippers on the arms, fastest dash allowed. A "gull" player swoops a scarf overhead to make the run honest. Reach the sea and you may swim in circles, shouting the good news.

Understanding check

Ask: "What two homes meet at the coast? Where does the mother lay her eggs? What do the babies do?" Sand-and-sea, a sand nest, dash to the waves — three answers and the lesson crawls safely home.

Parent tips

Keep the gull playful, never scary — the dash is a triumph story, and most hatchlings make it. If your child asks how the babies know where the sea is: the horizon glows brighter over the water, and the waves whisper. True, and just magical enough to retell.

Staying safe

Beach rules are turtle rules: swim between the flags with a grown-up, never turn your back on the waves, and if you ever find a real nest, look with eyes only — the sand nursery must not be touched.

This lesson pairs with the Turtle flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Animals & Their Habitats (Class 36).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · ANIMALS & THEIR HABITATS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Fish — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson opens the ocean — the biggest habitat on the planet — with its most numerous resident. The fish teaches the swap nobody can make: we breathe air, fish breathe water, and gills are the reason.

What is this?

The ocean is one enormous connected sea covering most of the Earth — deeper than mountains are tall, from sunlit shallows to the sandy floors. All of it is one address: every drop touches every other drop.

What does it mean?

Land animals carry their air around inside them; fish skip the carrying. Water pours in the mouth, washes over the gills on each side of the head — feather-red filters that grab the oxygen — and out it flows. Fins steer, the tail drives, and the whole body is shaped to slide through a home that has no floor you could trip on and no ceiling you could bump.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three ocean ideas: the ocean is the biggest habitat on Earth, bigger than all the land homes together; fish breathe the water itself through their gills — they would suffocate in our air; and fins and tails are their steering and engine.

Why this matters

Gills are the cleanest possible contrast lesson: same need, opposite solution. Once a child can say "we could never swap — I breathe air, the fish breathes water," they hold the deepest fact about habitats: the home and the breather must match.

What it teaches

Respiration basics in child words, scale thinking (biggest home on the planet), body-part function (gills, fins, tail), and humble awe — the ocean is too big to visit all of, and that bigness is the lesson.

Words to learn

fishoceangillsfintailwaterscale

Say this to your child

“"The fish lives in the ocean, the biggest home on the whole Earth. It does not breathe air like us — it breathes the water! The water runs in its mouth, through its red gills and out again. Its tail pushes and its fins steer. We could never swap homes."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is a fish, and this is its home — the ocean."
  2. Size it honestly: the ocean covers most of the globe — spin a globe or map and let the blue win. Biggest home, no contest.
  3. Do the gill story: behind each fish cheek sits a red, feathery filter. Water in the mouth, past the gills — out the sides. The fish is breathing the water itself.
  4. Try the swap-proof: pinch your nose and mouth gently for one second — we cannot breathe water; the fish cannot breathe air. Never swap. That is why the ocean is its home and ours is ours.
  5. Finish with the fins: steering wheels and engine. Then play gill-breathing (below).

Look closer at the picture

On this card a rounded blue fish with a pale belly, dark fins and a big friendly eye swims above a sandy seabed with a soft wave of water behind it. The word "ocean" sits below — one fish, gliding through the biggest room in the world.

Ask your child

"What does a fish breathe — air or water?" "Where are the gills?" "What do the tail and fins do?" "Which is bigger, the ocean or all the land?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "It breathes water through its gills," "The ocean is the biggest home on Earth!" or the swap line: "We couldn’t live there and it couldn’t live here — we breathe different things!"

Out in the real world

Aquarium walls and fish counters are gill theatres: watch the mouth open-shut rhythm and name it — "that is breathing, water edition". A globe’s blue share is the size lesson, repeatable every time the world map comes out.

Try it together

Gill pantomime: cheeks puffed, mouth open-shut in slow fish-breath, glide across the room with palms pressed together as the tail. Mid-game call the swap: "SWAP!" — everyone must gasp one big human breath and shout what they breathe. Air and water, two breaths, one game.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is the biggest habitat on Earth? What do fish breathe, and with what?" Ocean, water-through-gills — two giant answers and the lesson is deep enough.

Parent tips

Keep gills concrete: finger-draw the two cheek lines on your own face and your child’s — "gills here, filters here". If asked whether the ocean ever ends, give the honest size: from space the Earth is called the blue planet because the fish’s home is bigger than all of ours together.

This lesson pairs with the Fish flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Animals & Their Habitats (Class 36).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · ANIMALS & THEIR HABITATS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Dolphin — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson adds the ocean’s great twist: not everyone under the waves breathes water. The dolphin holds its breath like us, leaps to refill — and greets its family with a whistle that works like a name.

What is this?

Dolphins live in the open ocean and along the coasts, roaming in pods — chattering family groups that hunt fish, surf waves and leap in arcs that show their pale bellies to the sky.

What does it mean?

A dolphin is a mammal in a fish’s world: lungs, not gills. So life in the ocean is a rhythm — swim, swim, surface, BREATH, dive again. The leap is not showing off; it is breathing taken at speed. And each dolphin carries its own signature whistle — a sound it makes so others can call it, the closest thing in nature to having a name.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three dolphin ideas: dolphins breathe AIR with lungs, like us — they hold their breath underwater and leap up to refill; they talk in clicks and whistles, each dolphin with its own signature sound; and they swim in pods — families that stay together.

Why this matters

The dolphin completes the fish lesson: same ocean, two breathing plans — gills below, lungs leaping above. The signature whistle also gives children their first "animals have names for each other" moment, which is empathy-building of the strongest kind.

What it teaches

Breath-hold awareness (a real, feelable skill), mammal-fish contrast reasoning, sound-and-name concepts, and cooperative play — pods take turns, pods stay together, and so do good games.

Words to learn

dolphinbreatheleapblowholewhistlepoddive

Say this to your child

“"The dolphin lives in the ocean but breathes air, just like us. It swims, and swims, and then leaps up — hoo! — one big breath through the blowhole on its head, and down again. Its family calls it with its very own whistle."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is a dolphin, and this is its home — the ocean."
  2. Spring the twist: it lives in the sea but does NOT breathe water. Lungs, like yours! It holds its breath below and leaps up — whoosh — to breathe again.
  3. Find the blowhole: on top of the head, a little trapdoor for air. One jump can be one giant breath.
  4. Do dolphin talk: clicks and whistles. Every dolphin has its own signature whistle — call it, and it answers. A name made of sound.
  5. Play surface-and-breath (below), then close with the pod: dolphins travel together, eat together, breathe together.

Look closer at the picture

On this card a sleek grey dolphin with a pale belly, a friendly eye and a small beak-like smile arcs above rolling blue waves, its curved back and tail fin clear of the water. The word "ocean" sits below — mid-leap, mid-breath, exactly where a dolphin lives its best moment.

Ask your child

"Does a dolphin breathe water or air?" "Where is the blowhole?" "Why does it leap out of the water?" "What is a dolphin’s whistle like?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "It breathes air — it jumps up for a big breath!" "The hole is on top of its head," or the name line: "Every dolphin has its own whistle, like a name!"

Out in the real world

Breath rhythm is testable in the bath: how long can your child hold a comfortable breath? (Three to five seconds, cheerfully.) That number IS the dolphin’s problem, felt in miniature. At any aquarium or beach, the surface-leap watch becomes a breath count.

Try it together

Pod relay: crawl-swim across the carpet, then "surface" at set points — touch the wall, stand, one huge breath with arms up as the blowhole opens, back down and glide on. Rule of the pod: nobody surfaces alone — the whole family leaps together, breathes together and giggles together.

Understanding check

Ask: "Does a dolphin breathe water or air? What is the hole on its head called? What is its whistle for?" Air, blowhole, calling its name — three answers and the pod leaps on.

Parent tips

Give each family member a signature whistle on the spot — a two-note hum each — and use them for a day of calling across rooms. The dolphin’s naming idea converts into a family game with zero props, and every call retells the lesson.

This lesson pairs with the Dolphin flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Animals & Their Habitats (Class 36).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · ANIMALS & THEIR HABITATS · AGES 4–5 YEARS
