Whale — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson ends the ocean trio with scale: the whale is the largest animal that has ever lived on Earth — bigger than any dinosaur find — and it got that way by eating some of the smallest meals in the sea.

What is this?

Whales roam the whole ocean, from polar feeding seas to warm nursery bays. The biggest — blue whales — grow longer than three cars in a row, with hearts the size of a small armchair.

What does it mean?

Size like that runs on surprises. A whale breathes air at the surface through its blowhole — one mighty breath lasting minutes below. It sings — long, booming songs that travel whole seas, whale-to-whale. And the blue whale’s diet is among the tiniest: it gulps enormous mouthfuls of water and strains out clouds of shrimp-like krill, millions at a time. Biggest animal, tiniest meals, gentlest table manners.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three whale ideas: whales are the biggest animals that have ever lived — bigger than the dinosaurs we dig up; they breathe air at the surface through a blowhole, like the dolphin; and the biggest whales eat tiny krill by the million, strained from great gulps of sea.

Why this matters

Whales hand children their first true "wow beyond belief" fact that is also verifiable — and verifying it (pace it out, lie in it, fit the family inside) teaches the habit of checking wonder against reality. Big-and-gentle also stretches character thinking: the ocean’s giant is no one’s monster.

What it teaches

Scale measurement (pacing, comparing, lying inside the size), singing and sound-travel curiosity, food-chain inversion (biggest eats smallest), and calm confidence — giants are not scary when you know their manners.

Words to learn

whaleblowholekrillgiantsonggulpbaleen

Say this to your child

“"The whale is the biggest animal that has ever lived — bigger than a bus, bigger than the dinosaurs! It breathes at the top through its blowhole, sings songs that travel across the whole sea, and eats tiny little krill by the million. The biggest giant in the world is a gentle one."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is a whale, and this is its home — the whole wide ocean."
  2. Land the size slowly: the biggest animal that has EVER lived. Bigger than every dinosaur bone in every museum. Longer than a bus — often three.
  3. Breathe like a whale: one surface breath through the blowhole, then minutes below. (Same plan as the dolphin — the ocean has two breathing teams.)
  4. Sing the secret: whales sing songs that boom across whole seas to family far away. Deep water carries voices like nothing on land.
  5. Serve the surprise meal: the giant eats TINY food — a mouthful of sea, strained through baleen, millions of krill kept, water back out. Then pace the whale out, floor to hallway (below).

Look closer at the picture

On this card a deep-blue whale with a pale, ridged belly and a small kind eye glides above rolling waves, its long body and big tail fin filling the picture. The word "ocean" sits below — the giant itself, at ease in the only home big enough.

Ask your child

"Is the whale bigger or smaller than a bus?" "How does it breathe — gills or a blowhole?" "What does the biggest whale eat?" "Why does it sing?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "It’s the biggest animal EVER — bigger than dinosaurs!" "It breathes through its blowhole at the top," or the surprise line: "It eats tiny krill — millions of them, in one gulp!"

Out in the real world

Whale scale is floor-space fun: three parked cars nose-to-tail, one long school corridor, a whole swimming lane plus a bit. Museums with whale hangs deliver the wow vertically. Sound-travel talk works anywhere loud: cup your ears — in the sea, a whale’s song would beat any speaker.

Try it together

Whale-length: heel-toe the family down the hallway or pavement until you reach whale length (three car-lengths, or about twenty of your child’s steps). Lie down in your whale, nose to toes, arms out — the whole family fits inside one whale with room to spare. Then one family blowhole-breath, together, and a hummed two-note whale-song to send it swimming.

Understanding check

Ask: "Is the whale the biggest animal ever? How does it breathe? What does it eat?" Yes — ever, blowhole air, tiny krill by the million — three answers and the giant swims on.

Parent tips

Let the size fact stay enormous — do not sand its edges with "about as big as". Children this age treasure one impossible-but-true fact above all toys; "the biggest animal ever is alive right now" is the one worth lending them. If asked what whales say, hum low and slow: whale songs are felt in the chest before the ears.

This lesson pairs with the Whale flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Animals & Their Habitats (Class 36).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · ANIMALS & THEIR HABITATS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Penguin — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson travels to the white end of the Earth: the polar region, where the ground itself is ice. The penguin shows how a bird with no fur, no den and no trees still keeps warm — feathers, blubber, and each other.

What is this?

The polar regions are the freezing ends of the Earth — sea ice, ice shelves and water that would numb a finger in seconds. No trees grow, few land plants — the "ground" is white and the sea below is full of fish.

What does it mean?

The penguin’s warmth is layered. Outside: dense feathers, oiled and overlapping — a windproof coat. Under the skin: a thick blanket of fat called blubber. And when the wind really bites, penguins do the trick no single bird can: they huddle, hundreds deep, shoulders tucked, and slowly rotate so everyone takes a turn in the warm middle and nobody stays cold at the edge.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three polar ideas: the polar region is the icy end of the Earth, where the sea itself freezes; penguins are birds that swim with their wings instead of flying; and they keep warm with feather coats, blubber — and the famous huddle.

Why this matters

The penguin teaches warmth as cooperation: the huddle only works because everyone shares the cold edge. It also corrects the bird story — wings are not only for flying — and it hands families the fairest warmth game ever invented.

What it teaches

Insulation science at coat level (feathers, blubber, huddling), turn-taking ethics built into the rotation, swimming-versus-flying body reasoning, and cold-weather empathy — the outside-of-the-huddle seat is real.

Words to learn

penguinpolaricehuddlefeathersblubberwaddle

Say this to your child

“"The penguin lives in the polar region, where the ground is ice and the sea is freezing. Its feather coat and fat blanket keep it warm — and when the wind blows hard, the penguins huddle up tight and take turns in the warm middle. Nobody stays cold alone."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is a penguin, and this is its home — the polar region, where even the sea turns to ice."
  2. Meet the coat: thousands of tiny feathers, overlapping like roof tiles, plus a fat blanket underneath. The cold cannot get through either easily.
  3. Flip the wings: these are birds that gave up flying in the AIR to fly in the WATER — wings as flippers, faster than they look.
  4. Tell the huddle: when the wind howls, penguins pack together tight and take turns — cold penguins on the outside shuffle slowly to the warm middle, and warm ones take their turn at the edge. Sharing, in feather coats.
  5. Play waddle-slide-huddle (below) and close with the address: ice above, fish below, friends all around.

Look closer at the picture

On this card a black-backed, white-bellied penguin with an orange beak and feet stands squarely on a low white ice floe, calm and front-facing, pale sky and sea around it. The words "polar region" sit below — one bird, dressed for the coldest address there is.

Ask your child

"Why doesn’t the penguin freeze?" "What are its wings for?" "What do penguins do when the wind gets too cold?" "Who stands at the edge of the huddle — and what happens next?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "It has a feather coat and a fat blanket," "Its wings swim — it flies in the water!" or the huddle line: "They take turns — the cold ones go to the middle and warm ones go to the edge."

Out in the real world

Winter dressing becomes feather logic: coat = feather layer, jumper = blubber layer, hugging a grown-up = huddle. Ice in a drink shows the floe from below. And any bath-time raft of toys floating on the water is an ice floe waiting for a penguin passenger.

Try it together

Waddle-slide-huddle: waddle across the room, feet out, arms tucked — then belly-slide the final stretch onto a cushion floe. Call "WIND!" and everyone packs into one tight back-huddle, arms wrapped, shoulders touching. Rotate the huddle one slow turn so the edge players move toward the middle — fair shares, warm hearts, zero frostbite.

Understanding check

Ask: "Where does the penguin live? What keeps it warm — three things?" Polar region, feathers-blubber-huddle — one big answer in three parts and the lesson is warm through.

Parent tips

Honour the turn-taking explicitly: "at the edge, then the middle — everyone gets both." If your child asks whether penguins miss flying, give the swim answer proudly: they traded one sky for another, and theirs is full of fish.

Staying safe

Ice is for penguins: real frozen water is never for walking on, however thick it looks. Cold-weather dressing follows the penguin plan — layers first, hat always — and snowy play ends with dry clothes and warm hands.

This lesson pairs with the Penguin flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Animals & Their Habitats (Class 36).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · ANIMALS & THEIR HABITATS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Seal — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson stays in the polar region to meet the seal — the neighbour who is half-in and half-out of the water: sleek torpedo below the surface, contented loaf above the ice, wrapped in the sea’s warmest coat.

What is this?

Polar seas freeze at the top into floes and ice shelves while staying liquid below. Seals need BOTH: open water to hunt fish, and solid ice to haul out on — for resting, napping in the sun and raising pups.

What does it mean?

The seal’s secret is blubber: a thick layer of fat under the skin that works like a wetsuit the seal never takes off — holding body heat in the water that would freeze us in minutes. On the ice it flops and dozes; below it swims like a bullet, steered by back flippers, hunting by feel: its whiskers are so sensitive they read the water itself, feeling fish move in the dark.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three seal ideas: seals split their lives between ice (rest) and water (hunting); blubber — a thick fat layer — is their built-in warm coat; and their whiskers can feel fish swimming past in dark water, like fingers that read the sea.

Why this matters

The seal delivers the class’s best do-it-yourself science: the blubber-glove experiment is safe, quick and unforgettable. It also rounds the polar picture — penguin huddles on the surface, seal below it — showing one habitat hosting different answers to the same cold.

What it teaches

Insulation experimenting (blubber-glove test), touch-sensitivity concepts (whiskers as feelers), two-world scheduling (ice shifts and water shifts), and gentle body-play — the seal scoot is comedy with core strength in it.

Words to learn

sealblubberfloehaul outwhiskersflipperdive

Say this to your child

“"The seal lives in the polar region — it rests on the ice and hunts in the sea. Under its skin it wears blubber, a thick warm coat it never takes off. Its whiskers feel the water in the dark, so no fish swims past unnoticed. Half its life is a nap; the other half is a hunt."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is a seal, and this is its home — the polar sea and its ice."
  2. Split its day: below the water — torpedo, hunting fish; on top of the ice — a happy loaf, dozing in the sun. Both halves are home.
  3. Introduce blubber: under the seal’s skin sits a thick coat of fat called blubber — the reason icy water feels like a cool bath to it. We will test how it works in a minute.
  4. Meet the whiskers: each one is a feeler that reads the water. In the dark under the ice, a seal’s face finds fish by feel alone.
  5. Run the blubber-glove test (below), do the seal scoot, and close with the address: ice to rest, sea to hunt.

Look closer at the picture

On this card a silver-grey seal with dark spots, long whiskers and a gentle face rests on a low white ice floe, snowy peaks rising behind it on the pale sea. The words "polar region" sit below — hauled out, warm inside its coat, between two naps of its two-shift day.

Ask your child

"Where does the seal rest, and where does it hunt?" "What is blubber?" "What can its whiskers feel?" "Why can WE not swim in that water?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "It sleeps on the ice and eats fish in the sea," "Blubber is its warm coat — like a wetsuit!" or the whisker boast: "It feels the fish with its whiskers in the dark!"

Out in the real world

Cold-water feel: one hand in a bowl of cold water bare, the other inside a bag-glove — the temperature gap between protected and bare skin IS the blubber lesson, felt in thirty seconds. Winter coats, wetsuits and duvets are all family blubber once named.

Try it together

Blubber-glove lab: one hand bare, one hand inside a plastic bag lined with thick fat (shortening) or doubled mittens — both into bowls of icy water side by side. Count the seconds until the bare hand begs out while the blubber hand stays cosy. Then the seal scoot: flat on the tummy, push up on palms, flop forward three times across the room — hauling out, at home.

Understanding check

Ask: "What are the two halves of a seal’s day? What keeps it warm in freezing water? What do its whiskers do?" Ice-and-sea, blubber, feel the fish — three answers and the floe is occupied.

Parent tips

Run the glove test fairly — same bowls, same minute — so the result is the child’s discovery, not your claim. If asked whether blubber is heavy, answer honestly: yes, and that is fine — in water, heavy and floaty are friends. Seals sink to swim; the coat does double duty.

This lesson pairs with the Seal flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Animals & Their Habitats (Class 36).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · ANIMALS & THEIR HABITATS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Polar Bear — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson finishes the cold pair at the very top of the map: the arctic, and the biggest bear on Earth. The polar bear teaches camouflage at its purest — and patience as a hunting tool that works by staying still.

What is this?

The arctic is the frozen ocean at the North Pole: sea ice drifting in slabs and sheets over deep, dark water, months of winter dark, and snow from horizon to horizon.

What does it mean?

A white bear on white ice is nearly invisible — and invisibility is the polar bear’s whole hunting plan. Seals must breathe through holes in the ice; the bear finds a hole, sits down, and waits — still as the snow around it — sometimes for hours, until a nose breaks the surface. One swift paw, and the patient hunt ends. The ice is not scenery here; it is the kitchen floor, the road and the dining table at once.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three arctic ideas: the arctic is the frozen sea at the top of the world, all ice and snow; the polar bear’s creamy coat matches it so well the bear can vanish — camouflage in action; and it hunts by waiting, perfectly still, at the seals’ breathing holes.

Why this matters

The polar bear completes the camouflage thread started by the lion (tawny on gold) with its opposite number (white on white) — two hunters, two colours, one trick. And the breathing-hole vigil teaches stillness as strength: the mightiest hunter in the arctic wins by not moving.

What it teaches

Camouflage testing (hide-and-seek science), stillness stamina — genuinely hard and genuinely trainable at four — cold-region mapping (top of the globe), and respect for patience as a real skill, not a passive one.

Words to learn

polar beararcticsea icecamouflagebreathing holewaitstill

Say this to your child

“"The polar bear lives in the arctic, on the ice at the very top of the world. Its fur is the colour of the snow — so when it waits still as a statue by a seal’s breathing hole, nobody sees it coming. The biggest bear on Earth hunts by being patient."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is a polar bear, and this is its home — the arctic, the frozen sea at the top of the world."
  2. Find the bear trick: creamy fur, snowy background. Ask your child to squint — where does the bear end and the ice begin? That vanishing act is called camouflage.
  3. Tell the hunt: seals keep breathing holes in the ice, like front doors. The bear finds one, sits, and waits — silent, statue-still — until a nose pops up.
  4. Compare the hunters: the lion wears gold on gold, the bear wears white on white — different ends of the Earth, the same disappearing trick.
  5. Run the camouflage test and the statue game (below), then close with the map: find the top of the globe — that white crown is the bear’s whole country.

Look closer at the picture

On this card a big creamy-white polar bear with a long neck, dark eyes and black claws stands on a low slab of sea ice, pale sky and paler sea all around it. The word "arctic" sits below — the hunter standing in its own invisibility cloak.

Ask your child

"Why is the polar bear hard to see on the ice?" "What are breathing holes for?" "What does the bear do at a hole?" "Where on the globe is the arctic?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Its fur matches the snow — that’s camouflage!" "It waits by the seal’s breathing hole, very still," or the map line: "The arctic is at the top of the world!"

Out in the real world

Camouflage hunts work anywhere: count the white things against white walls, the brown things against fences — background matching, street edition. Globe time: trace from your home to the top of the world, and let your child place a finger on the bear’s country.

Try it together

Camouflage test: cut a paper bear in white and one in red. Hold each against the white wall, then a busy poster — which bear vanishes, which shouts? Then Statue Hunt: the "bear" must cross the room toward the "seal" (a cushion throne) moving ONLY when the seal’s eyes are closed — freeze when open. Reaching the seal earns the biggest growl of the day.

Understanding check

Ask: "Where does the polar bear live? Why can’t the seals see it? How does it hunt?" Arctic ice, fur matches snow, statue-still at breathing holes — three answers and the hunter rests.

Parent tips

Keep the hunt honest but gentle: the bear waits because seals are quick and holes are few — patience is not cruelty, it is the job. If your child asks whether the ice ever melts for the bear, answer truthfully and briefly: the arctic ice shifts with the seasons, and the bear follows the ice — the kitchen floor moves, and the bear moves with it.

This lesson pairs with the Polar Bear flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Animals & Their Habitats (Class 36).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · ANIMALS & THEIR HABITATS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Bat — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson closes the class with the strangest address of all: the cave, where the bat sleeps hanging by its feet through the day — then flies out at dusk to hunt the night using nothing but sound.

What is this?

A cave is a room inside rock: dark all day, cool in summer, still and sheltered — no wind, no rain, and no light at all past the entrance. To animals that sleep by day, that darkness is not scary; it is blackout curtains.

What does it mean?

The bat sleeps hanging upside down from the cave ceiling, folded in its own wings — feet grab, head drops, day over. At dusk it flies out and hunts in the dark by echolocation: it clicks, the sound bounces off moth or wall or tree, and the echo comes back a picture. Ears as eyes. The cave gives the day’s safe sleep; the night gives the hunt; the bat owns both shifts.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three bat ideas: bats rest in caves (and similar dark quiet spots) hanging upside down by their feet; they fly at night and find their way by listening to the echoes of their own clicks — seeing with sound; and they are the only mammals that truly fly.

Why this matters

The bat corrects two fears at once: caves stop being black holes (they are bedrooms) and bats stop being scary (they are pest-controllers with sonar). Ending the class on the animal that turned darkness into a superpower sends children to bed on the class’s bravest note.

What it teaches

Sound-and-echo physics in game form, fear-to-fascination conversion, upside-down body play with trusted grown-ups, and night-day scheduling — the third shift-worker of the class, after owl and fox.

Words to learn

batcavehangupside downechoclickdusk

Say this to your child

“"The bat lives in a cave and sleeps hanging upside down by its feet, all day long. At night it flies out and clicks — and the echoes bounce back, drawing a picture in sound: moth over there, wall over here. It sees with its ears! And every night it eats thousands of tiny bugs for us."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is a bat, and this is its home — the cave."
  2. Read the hang: feet up, head down, wings wrapped like a blanket. Upside down is bat-normal — and handy: drop the grip and flight starts by falling.
  3. Tell the ear-eyes: in pitch dark the bat clicks — tsk-tsk — and the echo bounces back. Moth here, wall there, friend overhead: a sound picture, better in the dark than our eyes are.
  4. Retire the scare: bats eat thousands of bugs a night — the night’s own pest control. Nothing about bats wants your hair; they hear it perfectly and steer away.
  5. Try the echo clap in a hallway, then play the echo game (below) and close the whole class: twenty-two animals, twenty-two homes, every one of them exactly right.

Look closer at the picture

On this card a soft grey bat with round ears, a smiling face and neatly folded wings hangs upside down from the rocky ceiling at the mouth of a cave, stones piled at the entrance below. The word "cave" sits below — the night worker, tucked into the quietest bedroom in the class.

Ask your child

"How does the bat sleep — right side up or upside down?" "What does it click, and what comes back?" "When does the bat fly out?" "What do bats eat at night?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "It hangs by its feet with its wings like a blanket," "It sees with its ears — clicks and echoes!" or the brave line: "Bats eat the bugs — they’re the night’s helpers!"

Out in the real world

Echoes are free: clap once in a stairwell, under a bridge, in an empty hall and listen for the bounce-back — that return is a whisper of the bat’s whole world. Dusk walks gain a mission: bats flicker against the evening sky exactly like fast swallows; point the flicker out and the night shift becomes visible.

Try it together

Echo-location, one-blindfold version: the "bat" sits blindfolded (eyes closed); the "moth" shakes a small box twice from somewhere in the room, then freezes. The bat points to where the sound came from — one click of the box per guess. Harder round: two moths, two corners. The room fills with listening. That is the cave’s gift: darkness worth navigating.

Understanding check

Ask: "Where does the bat sleep, and how? What does it use to hunt in the dark? When does it fly out?" Cave-upside-down, clicks-and-echoes, at dusk — three answers and the class is complete.

Parent tips

End on the tally, out loud, together: meadow, pond, woodland, forest, eucalyptus, bamboo, rainforest, grassland, savanna, desert, river, coast, ocean, poles, cave — the whole class in one breath, your child’s new map of where everybody lives. And if a bat fear lingers, the cure is the fact: a bat that hunts midges over a pond has zero interest in anything with a hairbrush.

This lesson pairs with the Bat flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Animals & Their Habitats (Class 36).

HABITAT WORKSHEET ACTIVITY · CLASS 36 · AGES 4–5

Desert Animals and Their Habitat — solve it right on the sheet.

Circle the desert survivors, match them to dunes, rocks and burrows, count the cacti and trace the word DESERT.

THE WORKSHEET — WRITE AND DRAW RIGHT ON IT

Your sheet is ready.

Pick a color or the eraser, then circle, match, count, choose and trace straight on the sheet with your finger, a stylus or the mouse. Press Save my work when you are proud — that is what marks this activity cleared for your child.

FOR GROWN-UPS

What this worksheet teaches.

What the child is learning: The desert is hot and dry, and the animals that live there are built for it — padded feet, big ears, burrows under the sand.

Knowledge to have ready: The word desert, and three desert residents your child can name on sight: camel, fennec fox and lizard.

Why this activity matters: Saying who does NOT belong is the fast route to understanding who does — the penguin and the bear make the desert definition sharp.

  • Habitat vocabulary
  • Sorting belong and not belong
  • Matching animals to homes
  • Counting to 4
  • Word tracing

What to say before you start: The desert is the hottest, driest home on the sheet — let us find the animals who can take the heat.

What to look for on the sheet: For the fennec fox ears — huge ears are desert air-conditioning, and your child will love knowing why.

Questions to ask along the way: Could the penguin live here? Why not? What would the camel say about all that ice?

Helpful hints without giving it away: Start with the camel — everyone knows that one — and let the other two circle themselves around it.

Parent tips: Sand in a tray plus a toy camel turns the matching row into a small world after the sheet is done.

Understanding check: Name one animal from the sheet that would hate the desert — and say why in your own words.

Real-life practice: On a hot sunny walk, ask: who is the camel of our neighborhood today?

HABITAT WORKSHEET ACTIVITY · CLASS 36 · AGES 4–5

Farm Animals and Their Habitat — solve it right on the sheet.

Circle the farm team, match cow, pig, hen and sheep to their homes, count the hay bales and trace FARM.

THE WORKSHEET — WRITE AND DRAW RIGHT ON IT

Your sheet is ready.

Pick a color or the eraser, then circle, match, count, choose and trace straight on the sheet with your finger, a stylus or the mouse. Press Save my work when you are proud — that is what marks this activity cleared for your child.

FOR GROWN-UPS

What this worksheet teaches.

What the child is learning: A farm is a habitat people built: every animal on it has a home with a name — barn, sty, coop, pen.

Knowledge to have ready: The farm team — cow, horse, pig, hen and sheep — and the word farm for the place they all live.

Why this activity matters: The farm is usually a child's first habitat with names for the homes themselves, which plants the idea that where you live has a word.

  • Farm animal names
  • Home vocabulary: barn, sty, coop, pen
  • Sorting belong and not belong
  • Counting to 5
  • Word tracing

What to say before you start: The farm is the one habitat with a barn in it. Let us get every animal home before supper.

What to look for on the sheet: For the lion sitting in the circle row — he does not belong, and catching him is the game.

Questions to ask along the way: Who sleeps in the barn? Who loves the mud? Which animal on this sheet have you seen for real?

Helpful hints without giving it away: The sheep is not in the circle row — she appears in the matching row, so keep her home ready too.

Parent tips: After the sheet, line up toy farm animals and build each home from blocks — the words come out on their own.

Understanding check: Ask where the pig lives, where the hen lives — two answers, no paper, real memory.

Real-life practice: Visit a farm or a petting zoo and find one home from the sheet in real life — barns count double.

HABITAT WORKSHEET ACTIVITY · CLASS 36 · AGES 4–5

Forest Animals and Their Habitat — solve it right on the sheet.

Circle the forest dwellers, match them to hollows, dens and thickets, count the trees and trace FOREST.

THE WORKSHEET — WRITE AND DRAW RIGHT ON IT

Your sheet is ready.

Pick a color or the eraser, then circle, match, count, choose and trace straight on the sheet with your finger, a stylus or the mouse. Press Save my work when you are proud — that is what marks this activity cleared for your child.

FOR GROWN-UPS

What this worksheet teaches.

What the child is learning: The forest is a home you can walk under: tall trees give food, shade and hiding places, and every forest animal uses them its own way.

Knowledge to have ready: The word forest, and three forest neighbors — squirrel, bear and deer — plus the fox who lives there too.

Why this activity matters: Forests are the habitat children meet in storybooks first; naming its residents turns familiar pictures into real knowledge.

  • Habitat vocabulary
  • Matching animals to homes
  • Sorting belong and not belong
  • Counting to 5
  • Word tracing

What to say before you start: Under the tall trees lives a whole neighborhood — let us meet who hides in the forest.

What to look for on the sheet: For the camel standing in the circle row — sand feet have no business in the woods, and that is the laugh of the sheet.

Questions to ask along the way: Who stores food in a tree? Who sleeps all winter? Where would you hide if you were small and furry?

Helpful hints without giving it away: The tree hollow and the bush are close together in the matching row — slow lines, no guessing.

Parent tips: On the next walk under trees, play spot-the-home: holes, nests, burrows all count.

Understanding check: Point at the deer: what does the forest give it to eat? Leaves and twigs is a right answer.

Real-life practice: Collect one fallen leaf on your next walk and call it forest mail — delivered to the fridge.

HABITAT WORKSHEET ACTIVITY · CLASS 36 · AGES 4–5

Ocean Animals and Their Habitat — solve it right on the sheet.

Circle who lives under the waves, match whale, clownfish and turtle to their ocean homes, count fish and trace OCEAN.

THE WORKSHEET — WRITE AND DRAW RIGHT ON IT

Your sheet is ready.

Pick a color or the eraser, then circle, match, count, choose and trace straight on the sheet with your finger, a stylus or the mouse. Press Save my work when you are proud — that is what marks this activity cleared for your child.

FOR GROWN-UPS

What this worksheet teaches.

What the child is learning: The ocean is the biggest habitat on Earth — and even inside it, animals split it up: the reef, the open water, the sandy floor.

Knowledge to have ready: The word ocean, and three ocean residents on the sheet: whale, clownfish and sea turtle.

Why this activity matters: Splitting one huge habitat into addresses — reef, open sea, seabed — is the first step from "fish live in water" to real ecology.

  • Habitat vocabulary
  • Matching animals to ocean homes
  • Sorting belong and not belong
  • Counting to 6
  • Word tracing

What to say before you start: The ocean is one home so big it has rooms inside it — let us find who lives where.

What to look for on the sheet: For the cow standing quietly in the circle row — dry land is her whole world, and that is the point.

Questions to ask along the way: Who breathes air but lives in the sea? (The whale — a real surprise.) Who paints the reef orange?

Helpful hints without giving it away: The seabed scene has seaweed on the sand — that clue separates it from the open blue water.

Parent tips: A bathtub becomes the open sea, a sponge the reef — retell the matching row with bath toys.

Understanding check: Name two animals from the sheet that could never live in the ocean — and one that could.

Real-life practice: At bath time or a aquarium visit, use the three ocean words: reef, open sea, seabed.

HABITAT WORKSHEET ACTIVITY · CLASS 36 · AGES 4–5

Polar Animals and Their Habitat — solve it right on the sheet.

Circle who thrives in the ice, match polar bear, penguin and arctic fox to their icy homes, count ice blocks and trace POLAR.

THE WORKSHEET — WRITE AND DRAW RIGHT ON IT

Your sheet is ready.

Pick a color or the eraser, then circle, match, count, choose and trace straight on the sheet with your finger, a stylus or the mouse. Press Save my work when you are proud — that is what marks this activity cleared for your child.

FOR GROWN-UPS

What this worksheet teaches.

What the child is learning: The polar regions are the coldest habitats on Earth, and their animals wear built-in coats — thick fur or a layer of fat.

Knowledge to have ready: The word polar, and three ice-ready residents: polar bear, penguin and arctic fox.

Why this activity matters: Extreme habitats make the matching rule obvious: nobody survives the ice without the right equipment, and the sheet shows exactly whose bodies have it.

  • Habitat vocabulary
  • Matching animals to icy homes
  • Sorting belong and not belong
  • Counting to 5
  • Word tracing

What to say before you start: The coldest homes on Earth belong to the warmest-dressed animals — let us meet the polar team.

What to look for on the sheet: For the monkey in the circle row — jungle arms would freeze in a minute, and your child will know exactly why.

Questions to ask along the way: What do polar bears and penguins both wear that we have to zip on? Who slides on their tummy?

Helpful hints without giving it away: Flat floating ice is the floe, tall pointy ice is the icebergs — say the two words and the match does itself.

Parent tips: Freeze a small bowl of water, slide the toy penguin on top, and the floe word becomes real.

Understanding check: Ask which is colder, our winter or the polar regions — then ask what the fox wears to be sure.

Real-life practice: Next snowy or cold day, one minute of penguin walking — wings in, tiny steps, the word polar said twice.

HABITAT WORKSHEET ACTIVITY · CLASS 36 · AGES 4–5

Wetland Animals and Their Habitat — solve it right on the sheet.

Circle who lives in the wetland, match frog, egret and crocodile to their soggy homes, count lily pads and trace WETLAND.

THE WORKSHEET — WRITE AND DRAW RIGHT ON IT

Your sheet is ready.

Pick a color or the eraser, then circle, match, count, choose and trace straight on the sheet with your finger, a stylus or the mouse. Press Save my work when you are proud — that is what marks this activity cleared for your child.

FOR GROWN-UPS

What this worksheet teaches.

What the child is learning: A wetland is land that is soaked — ponds, reeds and mud — and it is a dinner, a bath and a hiding place all at once.

Knowledge to have ready: The word wetland, and three wetland regulars on the sheet: frog, egret and crocodile.

Why this activity matters: The wetland is the habitat that is neither dry nor deep — naming it teaches children that habitats come in every in-between flavor, not just desert versus ocean.

  • Habitat vocabulary
  • Matching animals to wetland homes
  • Sorting belong and not belong
  • Counting to 4
  • Word tracing

What to say before you start: Where the water meets the grass, the wetland squelches — let us find who loves it that way.

What to look for on the sheet: For the duck — she is in the circle row but not the matching row, so she needs a circle and a wave goodbye.

Questions to ask along the way: Who hops and who wades? What does the crocodile use the mud for? Have you ever heard frogs at night?

Helpful hints without giving it away: The frog is the easy anchor — he lives half in the water and half on the lily pads.

Parent tips: After the sheet, jump like a frog, wade slowly like an egret and snap like a crocodile — three animals, three moves.

Understanding check: Name the three wetland homes without the paper: pond, reeds, burrow.

Real-life practice: Pass any pond or canal on your walks and ask: who from our sheet could live here?
